## Objectives

- Understand why averaging many bad trees gives one good model — and the one trick that makes it work
- Tell **bagging**, **random forests** and **boosting** apart in a sentence each
- Fit both, tune the two or three settings that matter, and read variable importance
- Lab: a churn model end to end, with a test error you would sign — and the same choice made for a hospital

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
On a table of customers, or of patients, this is the model that usually wins
:::

| | Predict | So that |
|---|---|---|
| **Telecom** | who cancels next month | the retention calls reach the customers about to leave |
| **Hospital** | who is readmitted within 30 days, who misses the appointment | the nurse's call, the reminder, the double booking reach the right patients |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,36,48]"}

- On such tables **gradient-boosted trees** win or tie almost every time; random forests come close with almost no tuning
- The price is the tree's one virtue: you can no longer read the model. Lecture 20 is about living with that

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Many trees {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The variance problem, and averaging

A single tree is unstable: high variance. Statistics has one universal remedy for variance — **average**.

$$
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat f_b\right) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{B} \qquad \text{if the } \hat f_b \text{ are independent}
$$

Fit $B$ trees, average their predictions (or vote), and the variance falls like $1/B$.

Except you have **one** training set. Where do $B$ independent trees come from?

## Bagging: bootstrap, then aggregate

1. Draw a **bootstrap sample**: $n$ rows *with replacement* from the training data
2. Grow a full, unpruned tree on it
3. Repeat $B$ times — 500 is typical
4. Predict by averaging (regression) or majority vote (classification)

Each tree sees about **63%** of the rows; the other 37% are *out of bag* for that tree. Predict those with it, and you get a test error **for free, without a test set**: the **OOB error**.

::: {.callout-note}
The bootstrap samples are not independent — they share most of their rows. So the trees are correlated, and the variance does not fall all the way to $\sigma^2/B$. That gap is what the next idea closes.
:::

## Random forests: one more trick

Bagging's trees look alike because they all grab the same strong variable at the top. Correlated trees average badly.

**At every split, consider only a random subset of $m$ of the $p$ predictors.** Typically $m \approx \sqrt{p}$.

- The strong variable is unavailable in most splits, so trees are forced to use others
- They become **decorrelated**, and the average gets much better
- That single line is the entire difference between bagging and a random forest

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
$m = p$ *is* bagging. `ranger` and `randomForest` default to $\sqrt{p}$. It is the one setting worth touching; try $p/3$ and $\sqrt p$ and keep the better OOB error.
:::

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} Monday's tree was one draw

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · Monday's data: trained on `Pima.tr` (200 women), tested on `Pima.te` (332)
:::

| Model | First split | Test error |
|---|---|---|
| 10 bootstrap trees | `glu` 8 times, `npreg` once, `age` once | 23.2–38.0% |
| Monday's tree, 4 leaves | `glu < 123.5` | 25.6% |
| Bagging, 500 trees, $m = 7$ | — | 25.6% |
| Random forest, 500 trees, $m = 2$ | — | 23.8% |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,44,22]"}

1. Ten samples of the same women: how many first questions? What does that say about *the* tree?
2. Tree 7 (root `age < 28.5`) scored 23.2%, better than the forest. Deploy it? One sentence.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Average the lottery

- **Three variables at the root** in ten samples, `glu`'s cut moving from 111.5 to 144.5, test errors from 23.2% to 38.0%: a single tree is one draw from a wide lottery, and Monday's tree was one of them
- **Averaging 500 draws** beats almost every draw: the forest is better than 9 of the 10 trees, and with five other seeds it stays between 23.5% and 25.0%
- **Forest against bagging** is close here: with 7 variables, five seeds give 23.5–25.0% against 24.1–24.7%. The big gain is averaging at all

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"No: I know tree 7 was the lucky one only because I looked at the test women; picked in advance, a single tree lands anywhere from 23% to 38%, the forest lands near 24% whatever the seed."
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Boosting {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Boosting: learn from the mistakes, slowly

Forests grow trees **in parallel**, each ignorant of the others. Boosting grows them **in sequence**, each one fitted to what the previous ones got wrong.

1. Start with $\hat f = 0$, residuals $r = y$
2. Fit a *small* tree $\hat f_b$ to the residuals $r$
3. Update: $\hat f \leftarrow \hat f + \lambda \hat f_b$, and $r \leftarrow r - \lambda \hat f_b$
4. Repeat $B$ times

Three knobs: **$B$** trees, **$\lambda$** the learning rate (0.01–0.1), **$d$** the depth of each tree (1–4).

::: {.callout-note}
"Gradient" boosting fits each tree to the *gradient of the loss*: for squared error, the residual itself. `xgboost` is this, with every engineering shortcut ever found.
:::

## Forest vs boosting, in one table

| | Random forest | Gradient boosting |
|---|---|---|
| Trees | deep, independent | shallow, sequential |
| Learns by | averaging away variance | correcting bias, step by step |
| Tuning | almost none — $m$, done | $B$, $\lambda$, $d$, and they interact |
| Overfits? | hard to make it | easy: too many trees, too big a step |
| Accuracy | very good | usually best |
| First choice | when you have an afternoon | when you have a week |

## In R — forest

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-3|5|7-8|10"}
library(tidyverse); library(ranger); library(ISLR2)
d <- Default |> mutate(default = factor(default))
set.seed(1); tr <- sample(nrow(d), 7000)

rf <- ranger(default ~ ., data = d[tr, ], num.trees = 500, importance = "impurity", probability = TRUE)

rf$prediction.error                                   # OOB Brier score: an error without a test set
sort(rf$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)       # which variables did the work

pred <- predict(rf, d[-tr, ])$predictions[, "Yes"]   # probability of default, held-out rows
```

## In R — boosting

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7-8|10"}
library(xgboost)

X   <- model.matrix(default ~ . - 1, d)              # numeric matrix, no intercept
y   <- as.numeric(d$default == "Yes")
dtr <- xgb.DMatrix(X[tr, ], label = y[tr])

par <- list(objective = "binary:logistic", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 3)
xgb <- xgb.train(params = par, data = dtr, nrounds = 300)

p_xgb <- predict(xgb, X[-tr, ])
```

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
`nrounds = 300` is a starting point: `xgb.cv(params = par, data = dtr, nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5)` finds the round where the test log-loss stops falling. Compare every model on the same held-out rows.
:::

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} Which model invites the patients?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · trained on `Pima.tr`, scored on the same 332 women of `Pima.te` (109 diabetic) · cut at 0.5
:::

| Model | Accuracy | Invited | Diabetic caught | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression | 80.1% | 89 | 66 | 0.866 |
| Monday's four-leaf tree | 74.4% | 82 | 53 | 0.728 |
| Random forest, 500 trees | 78.0% | 94 | 65 | 0.830 |
| Boosting, 60 rounds (`xgb.cv`) | 76.2% | 106 | 68 | 0.829 |

1. Which model ranks the women best? Which is the most accurate?
2. Every GP must be able to say why their patient was invited to the test. Which model do you deploy? Defend it in one sentence.

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} The baseline wins this one

- **Logistic regression** is best on both: 80.1% accuracy, AUC 0.866. With 200 women and 7 measurements there is little left for trees to find that a straight line on the log-odds misses
- **Forest and boosting** clearly beat Monday's tree (AUC 0.83 against 0.73), not the baseline. Boosting catches the most diabetic women, 68, by inviting the most, 106

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"The logistic regression: it ranks the women best, and every GP can be told which measurements raised the patient's risk and by how much; the forest would cost that explanation and buy nothing."
:::

["Boosting wins on tabular data" is a claim about thousands of rows. On 200, the baseline nobody may skip is the model to beat — today's lab checks it on 7 000.]{.muted}

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Lab {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Churn, end to end

`churn.csv` on Blackboard: 7 000 telecom customers, 18 predictors, `churn` yes/no.

1. Split 70/30, **stratified** on `churn` — it is 28.5% yes, and a random split can drift
2. Logistic regression: the baseline nobody may skip
3. Pruned tree — print it, read it
4. Random forest, default $m$; then $m = p/3$
5. `xgb.cv` to choose `nrounds`; then `xgb.train`
6. One table: model × {accuracy, AUC, log-loss} on the 30%
7. `variable.importance` from the forest vs the top splits of the tree: do they agree?

Deliverable: the table in step 6, and one paragraph on **which model you would deploy, and why the answer is not simply "the most accurate one"**.

## The same pipeline, in a hospital

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The deliverable's second paragraph: a 30-day readmission model, built step by step like this one
:::

| | Telecom · churn | Hospital · readmitted within 30 days |
|---|---|---|
| A missed case costs | a customer, and the revenue | a patient back in a bed, often sicker |
| A false alarm costs | a discount nobody needed | a nurse's phone call |
| Who must understand the score | the retention team | the ward's doctors and nurses, and the patient |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,30,40]"}

Same seven steps, same table of models. Would you deploy the same model, at the same 0.5 cut? Write the second paragraph: what changes, and why.

## Every tree in a forest is wrong. The forest is right because they are wrong in different ways.  {.statement}
